summary: Describes a method for compressing TCP/IP headers to improve performance over low speed serial links, with motivation, implementation, and performance results. It includes C code for a sample implementation. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1144 describes how two ends of a serial link can avoid resending most of a TCP/IP header on every packet. They store recent headers and send the changed fields, reducing repeated information on the link.

how does tcp ip header compression work

subtitle: Reduces repeated TCP/IP header data on slow serial links by sending only changes between packets.

tldr.problem: On a slow serial link, repeatedly sending the full TCP/IP header consumes capacity and delays interactive traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The link endpoints keep recent headers for each TCP conversation and encode a compact change mask, connection identifier when needed, checksum and differences.
tldr.outcome: The RFC reports an average compressed header of 3 bytes. Link framing detects corruption, and TCP retransmissions help restore synchronized header state.

today: RFC 1144 is a Proposed Standard published in February 1990. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its security section states that security considerations are not addressed.

sections.title: The Cost of Repeated Headers
sections.content:
RFC 1144 targets TCP/IP traffic over serial links running from 300 to 19,200 bits per second. A minimum TCP/IP header is 40 bytes, even when a user sends only a small amount of data. On a slow line, those repeated bytes consume capacity and can delay typed-character echoes while bulk data is in progress.

The design aims to reduce interactive and acknowledgement traffic enough to improve response. It compresses TCP/IP datagrams specifically; the RFC says its investigation found UDP/IP traffic was not a suitable target for this method.
sections.plainLanguage: Small TCP messages still carry full IP and TCP headers. On a slow serial connection, the repeated header bytes can take time that could carry application data.

sections.title: Remembering the Previous Header
sections.content:
Many header fields stay constant during a TCP conversation, while others change in predictable ways. Both ends of the serial link keep a copy of the most recent header for each active conversation. The sender can then describe the new header by naming the conversation and reporting changes instead of sending every field again.

The link ends use only state shared across that one link. The RFC treats each physical link as two independent one-way links, so the compressor does not depend on seeing every packet in the full TCP conversation.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver stores the last header for each conversation. The sender can refer to that saved header and send only the fields that changed.

sections.title: The Compressed Packet
sections.content:
A compressed packet contains a change mask, an optional connection number, the unchanged TCP checksum and values for fields marked as changed. The mask covers packet ID, TCP PUSH, sequence number, acknowledgement, window and urgent-pointer information.

Small positive changes from 1 through 255 fit in one byte. A zero byte signals a following 16-bit value. A change too large for that encoding causes an uncompressed packet to be sent. Special mask patterns represent common interactive echo and one-way data cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A mask identifies which header values changed. The packet then carries those changes and the TCP checksum, while the receiver fills the other fields from its saved header.

sections.title: Compressor and Decompressor Decisions
sections.content:
The compressor sends non-TCP packets, IP fragments, and packets with specified TCP control conditions as ordinary IP. When it has no matching saved connection header, or a field that should remain constant has changed, it sends an uncompressed TCP packet that updates the receiver's saved state.

For a compressed packet, the receiver selects the saved header, applies the encoded changes, restores the packet length, recalculates the IP header checksum and combines the header with the remaining data. Communication is one-way at the compression protocol layer; the decompressor does not send state updates back.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender uses ordinary packets when a header cannot safely be compressed. Otherwise, the receiver updates its saved header with the changes and rebuilds the IP packet.

sections.title: Detecting Errors and Resynchronizing
sections.content:
Compression removes redundancy that might otherwise expose line errors. RFC 1144 therefore requires link-level framing to detect damaged packets and tell the decompressor, which discards them. The TCP checksum also detects header-state errors that produce incorrect sequence numbers.

After a framing error, the receiver discards compressed packets until it sees an explicit connection number or an uncompressed TCP packet. TCP retransmission leads the compressor to send an uncompressed packet when it detects a retransmission, restoring the saved header state without a separate feedback exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: Link framing tells the receiver when a packet is damaged. After an error, the receiver waits for a packet that identifies the connection and restores the saved header.

sections.title: Configuration and Measured Performance
sections.content:
The implementation needs a set of saved-header slots. The RFC recommends 16 slots when the link cannot negotiate the number; negotiated configurations may use from 1 to 256. Each slot can hold a header up to 128 bytes. Compression can be disabled for links that cannot negotiate it.

The RFC compares header compression with general data compression and reports performance measurements on computers of its time. It gives an average compressed header size of 3 bytes and describes a design goal of 5 bytes. Its security section says that security considerations are not addressed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The link endpoints need enough saved-header slots for active TCP conversations. The RFC reports that the compressed header averaged 3 bytes in its described measurements.

items.desc: Carries the TCP/IP header and identifies the saved-header slot.
